source.title: LLM Strategic Reasoning: Agentic Study through Behavioral Game Theory
source.authors: Jingru Jia; Zehua Yuan; Junhao Pan; Paul E. McNamara; Deming Chen

record.file_problem: The full paper is present; some tables are flattened in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares a strategic-reasoning measure across differently sized models, which bears conceptually on downstream performance versus scale. It does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates strategic reasoning depth (τ) in games, not held-out cross-entropy loss, scaling exponents, compute-optimal allocations, or extrapolation. Its model-size statements and results bear only on V6. The LLaMA comparison rows below give one same-game, same-condition size contrast; the paper’s broader statement that smaller models sometimes match or outperform larger ones does not identify all corresponding model pairs and conditions.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates 22 off-the-shelf LLMs on a new downstream task: strategic reasoning depth τ in matrix games. It compares models of different sizes, including the LLaMA-3.1 8B/405B pair and the R1-distilled Qwen 1.5B–32B series, and concludes that size alone does not determine τ. This bears weakly on V6. It is not a controlled scaling sweep, and it does not touch loss, exponents, allocation or fitting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say model size is not the sole factor in strategic reasoning quality; context, model structure and training data likely matter. Their main conclusions are broader. Reasoning models (o1, o3-mini, R1) lead in τ. Longer chains of thought and CoT prompting do not reliably help. Demographic personas shift τ, revealing bias.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a behavioral-game-theoretic evaluation of strategic reasoning depth rather than measuring language-model loss or fitting scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Strategic reasoning depth varies by model and game type; the paper also reports effects of CoT prompts and demographic personas, but these are not scaling-law fits.
record.problems: The scale comparison is not a controlled scaling sweep; the reported measure is strategic reasoning depth rather than pretraining loss, and the table does not report uncertainty for the cited values.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional model-by-game τ values in Tables 3 and 7, but most do not have model sizes stated alongside the results or constitute explicit size contrasts. They were not extracted as evidence for V6. Other tables on CoT and demographic effects do not test the claim versions.

missing.what: LLaMA-3.1-8B vs 405B τ across all 13 game columns. The 8B model is higher in comp HS/LS, coop BL/HP, mixed BL/L-Pun and one incomplete-information column. The 405B model is higher in coop AP, mixed H-Pun and three incomplete-information columns. The fit log-likelihoods show which values are identified.

DeepSeek-R1-distilled Qwen size series (1.5B, 7B, 14B, 32B) τ by game. Competitive BL is 0.421, 0.120, 0.518, 0.790: 32B is highest, but the series is non-monotonic. The distilled LLaMA 8B vs 70B pair is also given.

record.verdict_notes: Scaling is peripheral to this paper. The model comparisons are across families with differing training. τ is unidentified wherever γ ≈ 0 and the fit is at chance, which is common for small models such as LLaMA-3.1-8B, so apparent small-beats-large cases may be artefacts. Treat the V6 verdict as weak. Hoffmann et al. is cited only in passing.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated strategic reasoning depth using the study’s game framework.
rows.baseline: LLaMA-3.1-405B: τ = 0.988, same game and variant
rows.note: The smaller model has higher τ than the 405B model in this condition, contrary to a simple monotonic scale-improvement expectation.
rows.check: LLaMA-3.1-8B's competitive-BL fit is at chance: log-likelihood −2.197 equals the 3×3 baseline (Table 13), and γ = 0.000 (Table 10). With γ = 0, choices are uniform whatever τ is, so τ = 1.298 is unidentified. It cannot show that the 8B model reasons deeper than the 405B model.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3.1-405B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated strategic reasoning depth using the study’s game framework.
rows.baseline: LLaMA-3.1-8B: τ = 1.298, same game and variant
rows.note: The larger model has lower τ than the 8B model in this condition.
rows.check: Its only contrast is R1's unidentified τ, so the size comparison can't be read. One game out of 13 also misrepresents the pair: across all games the 8B model has higher τ in about 8 and the 405B model in about 5.

relationships.condition: Strategic reasoning depth τ in one-shot matrix games, comparing uncontrolled off-the-shelf models of different sizes
relationships.reason: Based on the text and the missing contrasts, since R1–R2 can't be read. Within the LLaMA-3.1 pair, the larger model does not win in most games. The distilled Qwen series is non-monotonic: in competitive BL, 7B scores 0.120 and 1.5B scores 0.421. The authors state that smaller models sometimes match larger ones. Evidence is weak: there are no controls, small models' fits are often at chance, and no uncertainty is reported.
relationships.display_finding: The larger LLaMA-3.1 model did not win in most games, while distilled Qwen 7B scored 0.120 versus 1.5B's 0.421 in competitive BL; comparisons lacked controls and uncertainty estimates.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
